name: Risperidone + Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride
meta: Risperidone 2 mg + Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg; Risperidone 3 mg + Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg
Prescription-only fixed-dose combination. Components – Risperidone: Schedule H –
prescription only; Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride: Schedule H – prescription only
sections: White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), slightly soluble in water.

Risperidone: Developed by Janssen in the late 1980s; one of the first second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics after clozapine. First approval/introduction: US FDA 1993 (Janssen Pharmaceutica). Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride: One of the oldest synthetic antiparkinsonian agents; remains widely used for drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms and dystonia. First approval/introduction: US FDA 1949 (Parkinson's disease).
Risperidone 2 mg + Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg; Risperidone 3 mg + Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg

Risperidone can cause dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms (parkinsonism, akathisia, dystonia). Trihexyphenidyl, a central anticholinergic, counteracts these symptoms, improving tolerability and adherence. Routine prophylactic anticholinergic use is debated – reassess need regularly.

Risperidone Potent antagonist of serotonin 5-HT2A and dopamine D2 receptors; also blocks alpha-1, alpha-2 adrenergic and H1 histamine receptors. Balanced 5-HT2/D2 antagonism improves positive and negative symptoms with fewer extrapyramidal effects at usual doses. Receptor / target profile: Potent 5-HT2A antagonist (Ki 0.17 nM) and D2 antagonist (Ki 3.57 nM), with relatively strong 5-HT2A over D2 preference; also blocks alpha-1, alpha-2 and H1 receptors.

Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride Blocks central muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the striatum, restoring the dopamine–acetylcholine balance disturbed by dopamine-receptor blockade or dopamine loss. Reduces drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, tremor and rigidity. Receptor / target profile: Antagonist at all five muscarinic receptors with much stronger activity at M1 and M4.
Summary: Well absorbed (bioavailability ~70%); Tmax ~1 h. Metabolised by CYP2D6 to 9-hydroxyrisperidone (paliperidone), which is equally active. Active-moiety half-life ~20 h. Renally excreted.
Summary: Rapidly absorbed; onset within 1 h, peak 2–3 h, duration 6–12 h. Excreted mainly in urine.

Risperidone: With or without food; avoid alcohol.
Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride: Take with meals; avoid alcohol; ensure fluid intake in hot weather.
Risperidone: Weight, glucose, lipids; prolactin if symptomatic; blood pressure (orthostatic); EPS assessment; CBC if leucopenia history.
Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride: Intraocular pressure periodically on long-term use; cognition in elderly; bowel and bladder function.

Risperidone: Drowsiness, sedation, tachycardia, hypotension, EPS, QT prolongation. Supportive treatment with cardiovascular monitoring. Trihexyphenidyl Hydrochloride: Anticholinergic toxicity: hot dry skin, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia, delirium, hallucinations. Supportive care; physostigmine may be considered under specialist supervision.
Evidence derives from component trials (risperidone efficacy; trihexyphenidyl for drug-induced EPS).
Guidelines (WHO mhGAP, NICE) discourage routine prophylactic anticholinergic use – reassess need periodically.
Report breast changes, menstrual changes or sexual problems

Avoid hot environments and strenuous exercise in heat
Do not take more than prescribed (risk of misuse)
Report confusion or difficulty passing urine
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
